full_query:
A 43-year-old man presents to the emergency department with bright red blood in his stool this morning. He noticed this yesterday as well, but it was much scanter. The patient is otherwise healthy. He was celebrating his birthday last night and admits having "too much to drink" and vomited profusely overnight. He currently feels well and is not nauseous. He has no other significant medical history and does not take any medications. His temperature is 99.2°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 110/75 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Physical exam reveals a nontender abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Rectal exam reveals grossly bloody stool. Laboratory studies are ordered as shown below.

Hemoglobin: 12 g/dL
Hematocrit: 36%
Leukocyte count: 5,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 179,000/mm^3

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? (A) Erosion into a gastric vessel (B) Inflammation and infection of colonic outpouching (C) Malignancy (D) Submucosal esophageal tear (E) Vascular malformation

Choice A: Erosion into a gastric vessel: This typically presents as upper gastrointestinal bleeding with melena or hematemesis rather than bright red blood per rectum
Choice B: Inflammation and infection of colonic outpouching (Diverticulitis): This condition usually presents with abdominal pain, fever, and changes in bowel habits
It is less likely in a young, healthy individual without these symptoms
Choice C: Malignancy: Colorectal cancer could present with bloody stools, but it is less likely in a young patient without a significant medical history or other systemic symptoms

Choice D: Submucosal esophageal tear (Mallory-Weiss tear): This is commonly associated with vomiting and typically presents with bright red bleeding due to the tear in the esophagus or proximal stomach mucosa following forceful vomiting
Choice E: Vascular malformation (Angiodysplasia): This can cause gastrointestinal bleeding, but it typically presents in older adults and in more chronic or recurrent patterns
Given the patient's history of heavy alcohol consumption and profuse vomiting, a Mallory-Weiss tear is the most likely cause
This condition results from mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction due to forceful vomiting, leading to acute gastrointestinal bleeding with bright red blood
The most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is a submucosal esophageal tear (Mallory-Weiss tear)
